name: Quotefirst — RFQ triage desk for small machine shops
one_liner: An AI RFQ triage desk that watches a small machine shop's sales@ inbox, turns every emailed PDF/drawing/spreadsheet into a structured request, scores it against the shop's own machines and capabilities, and drafts a same-day "we can do this, here's the ballpark and when" reply.
problem: Small custom manufacturers (10-200 employees: machine shops, fab shops, injection moulders) take in RFQs as emails with PDF drawings, spreadsheets and BOMs into a shared sales@ or an owner's inbox. One or two experienced estimators handle everything, so quotes take 2-5 days and some RFQs are never answered at all. Buyers expect speed: a 2020 survey of 417 US part buyers found 67% expect a quote within 24 hours and 75% decide within a week of receiving one. The result is lost jobs for reasons that have nothing to do with price, and estimator hours burned on RFQs the shop was never going to win (wrong material, tolerance beyond machine capability, quantity too high, lead time impossible). Today the workaround is the estimator reading every email themselves, or an enterprise quoting platform the shop finds too heavy. Note: there is no credible published figure for how many RFQs small shops never answer — treat that as unproven and part of what the first pilots should measure.
target_customer: Owner or VP of Sales at a US job shop with 10-200 employees and 1-3 estimators (CNC machining, sheet metal, weldments, plastics). Buyer is the owner — they sign for $200-600/month tools without a committee. Secondary buyer: the lead estimator who keeps the tribal knowledge.
why_now: Vision-capable LLMs became cheap enough to read drawings and attachments at scale in the last year (Gemini 2.5 Flash at $0.30/$2.50 per million tokens with PDF pages billed as images; GPT-5 mini at $0.25/$2.00), so parsing a 12-page RFQ packet costs cents rather than dollars. Capital is validating the category rather than closing it: Uptool raised a reported $6M seed in Feb 2026 for small-shop AI quoting. And a bookmark pattern this week (@priya_vc on unstructured inbound → structured work orders, @maya_builds on YC W26's vertical back-office agents) says the winners pick one industry and own one workflow end to end.
comparables: Paperless Parts (paperlessparts.com) — the incumbent quoting platform: RFQ workflow, CAD/drawing analysis, costing rules, ERP integrations. No public pricing; a competitor's comparison page claims 10-12 week deployments and $1,000+/month, and Capterra/SoftwareAdvice reviewers cite click-heavy quote creation and cost. Gap: deployment weight and price exclude the 10-50 person shop. Uptool (uptool.com) — the closest direct competitor and the main threat: small-shop AI that reads emailed RFQs, drawings and BOMs and drafts estimates, published at $195-495/month, month-to-month, reported $6M seed Feb 2026. Gap: it is aimed at producing an estimate; our wedge is the decision before the estimate — quote / clarify / no-quote scored against this shop's machine list, tolerance limits and current backlog, so the estimator only touches winnable work. Toolraw (toolraw.com) and Zetisis (zetisis.com) score drawings and match capability, but on the buyer/marketplace side (matching buyers to suppliers), not as a shop-owned intake desk. Xometry and Fictiv are marketplaces — they bring demand but take the customer relationship, which is the opposite trade. RFQ AutoPilot (rfqautopilot.com) does email RFQ detection and extraction with a free tier, but aimed at distributors, not machining capability fit. Honest read: this is a contested category, not an empty one; the defensible narrow slice is capability-fit triage plus a same-day acknowledgement, not full cost estimation.
market_note: Estimate, stated as such. Census County Business Patterns counts establishments under NAICS 332710 (Machine Shops) — the right denominator to pull, though CBP covers employers only and 332710 understates shops classified elsewhere; free directories independently list thousands (EveryJobShop reports 3,769 companies, Kerfgrid 7,079 shops across 10 states as of Oct 2026). At a conservative 20,000 US shops in the 10-200 employee band and a $400/month price, that is roughly a $96M/yr US-only SAM; a credible first target is 300 shops / ~$1.4M ARR. Willingness to pay is evidenced by Uptool's published $195-495/month and Paperless Parts selling above that to larger shops. Do not quote the "78% buy from the first responder" statistic — research shows it comes from cross-industry lead-response work, not manufacturing.
risks: Uptool is already in this exact buyer's inbox with a $6M seed and a cheaper-than-Paperless price; if they ship capability triage as a feature, the wedge closes. Accuracy on real-world scanned prints may be far below demo quality, and in manufacturing one bad recommendation destroys the trust the whole product depends on. Shops are slow, relationship-driven buyers with low software budgets and real ITAR/data-sensitivity objections, so sales cycles may be longer than the economics of a $400/month product can support without channel partners.
riskiest_assumptions: 1) That capability-fit triage, not price estimation, is what the owner will pay for — if the shop only values the dollar number, Uptool and Paperless Parts have already taken that ground and we are a feature. Fragile because estimators may say "I can tell in 20 seconds whether I can make it." 2) That drawing extraction is accurate enough on real scanned, hand-annotated prints to trust a no-quote recommendation; a single wrongly rejected $200k job kills trust permanently (mitigation: never auto-reject, only rank and pre-fill). 3) That shops will grant mailbox access (Google Workspace/Microsoft 365 OAuth) to a vendor they just met, and that ITAR/defence work does not immediately force an on-prem story.
first_customers: Ten shops sourced by hand, not by ads: (a) scrape 50 shops in one metro from EveryJobShop and Kerfgrid filtered to CNC machining with 10-200 employees, call the number on the site and ask for the owner; (b) the r/Machinists and r/Manufacturing communities, plus Practical Machinist forums, where quoting-time threads recur; (c) walk the floor at a regional show (IMTS/Fabtech regional events) — owners attend personally; (d) reply to @hardwarehank's thread and DM the shop owners in the replies. Target one metro so references compound and onsite setup takes an hour.
validation_test: This week: ask 5 shop owners to forward you the last 20 RFQ emails they received (redacted as needed). Run them manually through Gemini 2.5 Flash with a capability profile you built from a 15-minute phone call about their machines, tolerance limits and materials, and send each owner a one-page triage sheet: rank, quote/clarify/no-quote, extracted line items, and a draft acknowledgement email. Pass = at least 3 of 5 owners agree the ranking matches what they would have decided AND at least 2 commit to a $400/month paid pilot (card on file, 30 days). Fail = owners say "I already know this instantly" or disagree with more than a third of the no-quote calls.
build_plan: Narrowest first version, 4-6 weeks: (1) 15-minute intake call produces a capability profile — machine list, max envelope, tolerance floor, materials yes/no, min/max quantity, current lead-time weeks — stored as a simple JSON per shop. (2) Google Workspace/M365 OAuth read-only on one mailbox (sales@), poll for new mail with attachments. (3) Per RFQ: extract attachments (PDF, XLSX, STEP metadata, images) and send to Gemini 2.5 Flash with structured output — customer, part name/number, quantity, material, finish, key tolerances, due date, ambiguities. (4) Score against the capability profile into quote / clarify / no-quote with the specific reason cited and a pointer to the page/field it came from. (5) One web page: today's RFQ queue, ranked, each row expanding to extracted fields plus a draft reply the owner edits and sends in one click (acknowledgement + clarifying questions, not a price). (6) Weekly email: what came in, what was answered, median response time. CUT from v1: any cost/price calculation, ERP or MRP integration, CAD geometry analysis, multi-mailbox and multi-user roles, customer portal, auto-send of anything.
reasoning:
Venture: Quotefirst won because the pain is expressed and quantified by buyers themselves (67% of 417 surveyed part buyers expect a quote inside 24 hours), the buyer is a single owner with signing authority, and the narrowest version — triage and acknowledgement, no pricing — can ship in weeks. It beat the dental AI receptionist idea, which I researched and found genuinely closed: Weave (public co., bought TrueLark for $35M), NexHealth ($125M Series C), Arini, Dentina and a dozen others already sell exactly outbound AI calling to independent practices at or below the price a new entrant could charge. It beat the travel-nurse credentialing venture because Kamana already ships a free clinician credential wallet plus a paid agency portal, and Reddit evidence says agencies resist third-party document access — the wedge is occupied and the real blocker is policy, not software. Gap is scored only 6 and the verdict is watch, not dig_deeper: Uptool is in this exact inbox with $6M and published $195-495/month pricing, so the whole thesis rests on capability-fit triage being a separable product rather than a feature they ship next quarter. That is precisely what the validation test checks.

Build: Compactly is a different problem, audience and workflow from the venture (an individual nurse planning her own next contract, versus a shop owner triaging inbound sales) and comes from a different bookmark. It scored 6.2 — filed, but honestly a modest build. Research found NCSBN's own free Nurse Licensure Guidance tool already answers "can my license cover state X", so the freshness and the wedge are not the compact map itself; they are joining compact status to the credential expiry dates read out of the nurse's own photographed documents, producing one personal, screenshot-shaped answer. No free tool found does that join: GoodStanding, HealthTasks, CerTracker and NurseCred track expirations but say nothing about where you can work; NCSBN says where you can work but knows nothing about your BLS card expiring mid-contract. Pain is latent — nurses live with this as scattered folders and recruiter texts rather than naming it — and what would make them notice it is the specific moment the tool dramatizes: a credential expiring in week 9 of a 13-week contract. Dropped as weaker builds: a release-notes generator (git-cliff, release-please, GitHub's built-in generator and Atlassian Rovo all do this free and well) and a Stripe payout explainer (audience overlaps nothing in the bookmarks worth a weekend, and finance people will not paste payout data into a stranger's page).

Two candidates were dropped before research as too close to companies named in the bookmarks: a Stripe-to-QuickBooks reconciler (that is LedgerLoop, the bookmark itself) and a generic vertical back-office agent (that is the nine YC W26 companies @maya_builds described).
candidates_considered:
VENTURE — Quotefirst, RFQ triage desk for 10-200 employee machine shops: KEPT. Expressed pain, single decision-maker, buyer-side evidence on 24-hour quote expectations, narrow first version possible in weeks. · Dental confirmation/recall AI agent for independent practices (from @dentalops_raj): DROPPED after research — Weave (acquired TrueLark for $35M), NexHealth ($125M Series C), Arini, Dentina, Resonate and others already sell this to the same 1-3 location practice with PMS integrations; no defensible gap at a price a newcomer could charge. · Travel-nurse credentialing / portable credential file (from @nomad_nina): DROPPED as a venture — Kamana already offers a free clinician wallet plus paid agency portal and was acquired by Triage; Reddit evidence shows agencies resist third-party credential access for privacy and workflow reasons, so the blocker is policy, not software. · Multi-processor payout reconciliation for marketplaces/agencies (from @ledgerloop_ana): DROPPED pre-research as effectively the bookmarked company's own stated inbound, and Synder/Bookkeep already cover it. · Quarterly release-notes platform (from @tired_pm_lee): DROPPED as a venture — crowded (Released at $1.10-1.70/user/mo, LaunchNotes, Beamer, AnnounceKit) and Atlassian Rovo now drafts release notes natively inside Jira.

BUILD — Compactly, drop your credential photos and see where and how long you can work: KEPT. One input, one personal map-shaped output, no good free equivalent found, ships in a weekend with browser-only BYOK Gemini. · ChangelogSmith, paste Jira/Slack mess → customer-facing changelog: DROPPED — git-cliff, release-please, GitHub's built-in release notes and Rovo already do this free and are well known to the exact audience. · Payout Explainer, drop a Stripe payout CSV and see gross/fees/refunds/disputes reconstructed: DROPPED — low shareability, finance users will not paste real payout data into an unknown page, and Stripe's own payout reconciliation report covers it. · Machine shop map from Census CBP 332710: DROPPED — EveryJobShop and Kerfgrid already publish free browsable shop directories, and it shares the venture's audience, which the two-different-problems rule forbids.
research_notes: 18 tool calls: 3 reading-equivalent context queries, ~9 venture, ~6 build (no images in tonight's bookmarks, so the reading pot went to link-free context). What changed because of research: (1) The dental idea started as my front-runner and died on a single Perplexity pass — Weave's $35M TrueLark acquisition and NexHealth's $125M Series C, plus a follow-up showing Arini/Dentina/Resonate all selling Open Dental-integrated AI recall, meant the same buyer is already served at a fair price. (2) Travel-nurse credentialing looked wide open until a Reddit-sourced summary surfaced Kamana (free nurse wallet + paid agency portal, acquired by Triage) and nurse comments that agencies refuse third-party document access — so I moved that bookmark from the venture track to the build track and narrowed it to the nurse's own planning decision. (3) The manufacturing idea was reshaped twice: finding Uptool ($6M seed Feb 2026, published $195-495/mo, same emailed-RFQ-to-estimate workflow) closed the obvious pricing wedge, so I moved the product to the decision *before* the estimate — capability-fit triage against the shop's own machine list — after a targeted search confirmed Toolraw and Zetisis do capability scoring only on the buyer/marketplace side, not as a shop-owned intake desk. (4) I checked and discarded two statistics I would otherwise have quoted: the "78% buy from the first responder" and "30% never respond" figures both trace back to cross-industry lead-response studies, not manufacturing; the defensible number is the 2020 survey of 417 part buyers (67% expect a quote within 24 hours). (5) API costs verified for both prototypes: Gemini 2.5 Flash $0.30/$2.50 per million tokens with PDF pages billed as images, GPT-5 mini $0.25/$2.00. (6) For the build, I confirmed NCSBN's free Nurse Licensure Guidance tool and the 43-state NLC list exist (so the map alone is not novel), that no free downloadable NLC+fees dataset exists (so the data must be hand-compiled with last-checked dates), and that GoodStanding/HealthTasks/CerTracker/NurseCred track expirations but do not answer the "where can I work next" question — which is the join Compactly makes.
prototype_summary: An interactive Quotefirst prototype that contrasts a chaotic shared sales@ inbox with a ranked, auto-triaged RFQ queue — complete with extracted fields, rule-based verdict explanations, editable draft replies, and a live shop-profile tolerance edit that flips an RFQ from CLARIFY to QUOTE.
